author: dusan-nikolic
description: In 1947, a Dutch painter stood trial for selling a Vermeer to Göring. To escape the death penalty, he had to convince the court that the painting was a fake, and that the forger was him.

hero.hook: Charged with treason for selling a masterpiece to the Nazis, he had only one defense: proving he had painted it himself.

blocks.text: On **October 29, 1947**, reporters crowded into an Amsterdam courtroom. A wealthy painter, [[Han van Meegeren]], was on trial as a Nazi collaborator. The main charge: selling [[Hermann Göring]] a priceless painting by [[Vermeer]] during the occupation.

His defense was a confession: he had painted that Vermeer himself. He also claimed to have made the *Supper at Emmaus* in the Boijmans Museum in Rotterdam. [[Abraham Bredius]], the leading Vermeer expert, denied it: for him, it was a genuine early work by the master. Facing the death penalty, Van Meegeren had to overturn a verdict the art world had already accepted: to save his life, prove he was a master forger.

At the trial, Van Meegeren claimed he had turned to forgery after the critics destroyed his career, at his solo exhibition of **1922** in The Hague. Despite skillful brushwork, his biblical subjects had failed to draw any positive reaction. But that version tidied up reality: as early as **1920**, he had already tried his hand at fraud.

Yet this painter in his twenties had a promising career ahead of him. In **1921**, his drawing of Princess Juliana's pet deer became a symbol of the Dutch people's affection for their royal family. In the mid-1920s, his portraits of high-society figures sold well. Despite that potential, he abandoned the artist's path.

Van Meegeren painted his Vermeers on genuine 17th-century canvases, with natural pigments true to the period. He mixed them with liquid [[Bakelite]], a synthetic plastic that, once dry, behaved like oil paint. His technique thus passed every scientific analysis of the 1930s.

blocks.caption: The Supper at Emmaus, the fake authenticated by Bredius and kept by the Boijmans Museum in Rotterdam.

blocks.text: Copying the 17th-century look was not enough: his paintings had to give the public what it wanted. Van Meegeren played on an unproven hypothesis of art historians: that Vermeer had gone through an early biblical phase. In the 1920s and 1930s, collectors were waiting for a new Vermeer to surface. Van Meegeren was happy to oblige.
Van Meegeren did not stop at Vermeer. His fakes also include works passed off as Frans Hals, Gerard ter Borch and Pieter de Hooch.

sections.title: The recipe for a fake Vermeer

blocks.text: The fake Vermeer sold to Göring was titled *Christ and the Adulteress*. [[Alois Miedl]], Göring's financial advisor, played a decisive part in the purchase. He brought in experts who, without a single chemical analysis, declared the painting genuine. Miedl shipped it to Berlin, something Van Meegeren had not anticipated: he had meant to sell it to a Dutch collector, not to a Nazi leader.

blocks.caption: Christ and the Adulteress, the fake Vermeer that entered Göring's collection.

blocks.text: Göring examined the canvas in turn and confirmed it: a genuine Vermeer. He reserved a place for it in the grand gallery of [[Carinhall]], his estate near Berlin. Before paying, however, he demanded documents on the painting's origin. Van Meegeren and Miedl persuaded him that they would reveal the owner's name, an imaginary figure, **two years** after the sale. For a Nazi leader keen to be able to shift the blame if things went wrong, that was enough.

By painting a new "Vermeer," Han van Meegeren proved his technique. The treason charge was dropped. His Vermeers lost all their value. Sentenced to **one year** in prison for fraud, he died of heart failure **two months** after the trial opened. The press proclaimed him a folk hero, the man who had swindled Göring: his real ties to the Nazis no longer interested anyone.

blocks.caption: The Amsterdam trial, 1947: the fake Vermeers displayed as evidence.

blocks.text: After the war, a journalist found a book of Van Meegeren's drawings in Hitler's library, with a handwritten dedication: "To my beloved Führer in grateful tribute, from H. van Meegeren, Laren, North Holland, 1942."

Today, Van Meegeren is counted among the most gifted forgers of the 20th century, at the intersection of public image and historical reality. His fakes warn against uncritical appraisals and definitive opinions, and they raise a question: how do we decide what a work is worth?
To escape the death penalty, Han van Meegeren had to prove he was a forger, and the press turned the suspected collaborator into the hero who had swindled Göring.

sources.text: J. Lopez, The Man Who Made Vermeers, Mariner Books, 2008, p. 5, 14, 54, 92-97, 126, 197-217 et 250.
